title: Transformed by Fire
author: Roger Peet
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/1000029642-680x453.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/19/the-
big-burn/)

I stood at the trailhead for a long time, pacing back and forth, returning to
the car, getting into it, starting it, turning it off again, getting out and
walking to the place where the trail left the gravel of the parking lot and
headed off into the manzanita scrub. I couldn’t make up my mind.

I was parked in a flat circle of gravel in a saddle overlooking a deep valley
on the edge of the Kalmiopsis wilderness in the southwestern corner of Oregon.
It was early, with the chill of a spring dawn at 4000 feet still lingering in
the clear and cloudless air. All around me, the silvery trunks of dead fir
trees rose, branchless and barkless, smooth grey cylinders emerging from deep-
green hummocks of manzanita and tanoak. The dead trees descended the slope in
front of me and rose again on the far side. They appeared on the slope up to
the next ridgeline and to the one after that, and again beyond that to the
horizon. In a 180-degree arc before me, there was barely a single living tree
to be seen.

The Kalmiopsis Wilderness is the second-largest wilderness area in Oregon, and
a landscape utterly transformed by fire. Nearly the entire wilderness burned
in the catastrophic Biscuit fire of 2002, and fifteen years later it burned
again in 2017’s Chetco Bar fire. The ranks of denuded slopes I could see from
the trailhead parking lot were bare to a degree you don’t see in many
landscapes in the mountains of Oregon, with the soil and stones visible
beneath what was once a steep, mature old-growth conifer forest. The forest
that once cloaked these dramatic mountains was completely obliterated twice. I
was having a hard time convincing myself to enter the wilderness and to see
the totality of that destruction for myself.

It was spring, and I was here for wildflowers. Every year, when the weather
starts to warm, I head out from Portland as often as I can to pursue the new
bloom of spring across the West. With the flowers come the insects, and the
birds aren’t far behind, and the surge of life back into the dull temperance
of winter consoles me greatly in these deeply stupid and fractious times.
Standing at the edge of the annihilated Kalmiopsis, I felt as if I were about
to embark on a weekend of missing out and confronting disaster rather than the
biological luxuriance I have come to rely on.

I somehow convinced myself to go through with it, and I left the lot and took
the trail lined with low bushes and scrub, my peripheral vision dopplering
through the silvery trunks. Before I reached the ridge, a bluebird was hopping
from severed limb to severed limb in front of me, blinking in and out of sight
between the trees, auguring some possibility.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/1000029558-680x907.jpg)

In the heart of the burn zone. Photograph by Roger Peet.

I rose along the rim trail to a high slope and emerged from the boluses of
manzanita into a barren dome of weathered serpentine rock. I could see further
into the wilderness at this point, and I could make out the point where the
scars of the Biscuit and Chetco Bar fires met, the point where even the
standing dead trunks of firs had been consumed. I crossed the dome, continued,
then stopped and turned back. I walked out into the expanse of rough, silvery
scree and looked around. Low to the ground, curved, straplike, leathery
leaves, and I knelt next to a patch of them and bent a finger under a rouged
bell to lift and reveal the vivid yellow of bright, pollen-covered pistils. A
fritillary, dwarfed, and another, and another. Beyond that, tiny stalks
bearing miniaturized larkspur flowers, a plant that in rich soil can reach six
feet in height. Beyond that, a thick vegetable mass of yellow asters, and the
flat mosaics of dwarf pussypaws, their furry pink involucres folded into
delicately hirsute spheroids, waxy leaves shimmering in the rising light. The
barren dome was a carpet of small blooms. I rose and turned. I was surrounded.

Serpentine rocks are relics of an ancient ocean floor pushed upward to the
surface by plate tectonics. They’re composed of ancient igneous rock
assemblages that contain high concentrations of metals such as magnesium, as
well as rarer ones like chromium and nickel. The presence of these metals in
high concentrations makes life difficult for plants growing on serpentine,
with the result that plant communities in areas dominated by serpentine show
surprisingly high levels of endemism- meaning that they are unique to the
area. The serpentine soils of the [Kalmiopsis
Wilderness](https://klamathforestalliance.org/the-klamath-siskiyou-region/)
yield the highest rates of plant endemism in Oregon, formed as deep-marine
crusts intruded from the depths of the earth over millions of years into
regions with established plant communities. The communities that found
themselves marooned on the new serpentine soils had to adapt or perish, and
those that succeeded formed new species found nowhere else on the planet.

Satisfied now that I’d made the right choice, I proceeded into the wilderness.
The rim trail descended after a couple of miles to meet an old roadbed, where
a path through thick manzanita was sometimes hard to follow. I found myself
stooping and kneeling every thirty feet to encounter some small flower or to
pursue a microscopic grasshopper into a thicket of blooms. The roadbed
followed a dogleg along the slope and crossed over into another watershed,
where the full extent of the double burn could be seen.

It had a dramatic effect. The catastrophic Biscuit fire had killed much of the
forest in the wilderness, including ancient stands of old-growth pines, firs,
and hemlocks, but many of those trees had remained standing. So many, in fact,
that in the years following the fire, the Forest Service allowed logging in
less protected regions surrounding the wilderness, prompting fierce resistance
from local communities who fought each other in the forests and on the ridges
over the industrial extraction of the remnants of the forest killed in the
fire. This was salvage logging, permitted under the liberal Clinton
administration to circumvent federal protections for wilderness buffer zones.
I had made camp on the ridge in a field of massive ancient stumps logged after
Biscuit, in a period when forest defenders blockaded the roads into the forest
to prevent commercial extraction. Logging damages all forests, but logging the
deadwood of ancient trees in a region with harsh, limited soils has lasting
consequences. The minerals and materials that make up those dead trees would
eventually return to the soil and produce a new generation of forest, but only
if they are allowed to remain. Research conducted on the burn scar after the
Biscuit fire [revealed](https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/salvage-logging-
replanting-increased-biscuit-fire-severity) that it was actually a previous
generation of salvage logging that had contributed to the fire’s severity.

Deep in the heart of the burn, I found a seep of water crossing the trail, and
in the wet soil surrounding the small pod it produced were hundreds of
Darlingtonia plants. Darlingtonia californica, also known as the Cobra Lily
(although it’s not a lily), is a carnivorous plant with strange, snakelike,
hooded leaves that enclose traps of sugary water in which insects drown and
are digested. Another regional endemic, these plants use their carnivory to
adapt to the harsh, thin, poisonous soil; where they appear, they are found in
profusion, covering marshy areas in nodding thickets of serpentlike leaves.

The harsh soils of the Klamath Mountains are under threat from more than just
fire: the recent surge in the price of and demand for nickel has mining firms
circling like vultures around the mountains and valleys of the rugged
Siskiyous. Canadian firm Homeland Mining has been buying up mining claims
along the eastern border of the Kalmiopsis wilderness, including the popular
hiking destination and botanical interest area of 8 Dollar Mountain, just
outside the small town of Selma. Homeland is interested in the nickel laterite
deposits present in the region’s serpentine soil complex, and if the decimated
forests and bleeding landscapes of Indonesia are any warning, then the
communities of Southern Oregon have their work cut out for them to preserve
their drinking water, their biodiversity, and the complex forest assemblages
that make their region unique. Local environmental organizations like KS Wild
and Kalmiopsis Audubon are [monitoring](https://www.kswild.org/mining-threats)
the advance of mining claims, and as the demand for data centers and for the
nickel ores that make them possible rises, they will need all the help they
can get.

I climbed up and out of the burn into a remnant pocket of ancient forest on
the south side of Canyon Peak. Massive old-growth firs and pines towered
overhead, while the odd saprophytic plants known as pine-drops reared their
hot-pink stalks out of the bone-dry duff. It was cool and shady after the
long, hot ascent, and I imagined what it must have been like here at the edge
of the massive fire that devastated the wilderness, watching the valley full
of 800-year-old trees disappear in a cloud of ash. Scientists suggest that the
fire ecology of this region may herald its transformation into a botanical
complex where trees give way to shrubs, and a new and more arid environmental
context comes to hold sway over the crags and defiles of the Kalmiopsis
region. For now, the forest endures, despite all the threats the future seems
to hold.
